pages.text: Long ago, a king was so bitter from betrayal that he had decided to marry a new wife each night and have her executed in the morning, so that she could never betray him. A young woman named Scheherazade asked to be married to him. Her father begged her not to. She was determined.

image.note: Illustration: Scheherazade before a king on a throne, calm and unafraid, lit by candlelight

pages.text: On the first night, Scheherazade began to tell a story. It was so brilliant, so full of wonder and mystery, that the king could not bear to have her executed before he found out how it ended. He postponed the execution by one day. That night, Scheherazade ended the story at the most gripping moment and began another. Night after night, story after story, Scheherazade told tales that were always more extraordinary than the one before. After one thousand and one nights, the king had forgotten his bitterness entirely. He asked Scheherazade to be his queen.

The stories she told are collected in a book called One Thousand and One Nights, sometimes called the Arabian Nights. They come from many sources: Persian, Indian, Egyptian, and Arabic storytelling traditions, gathered and shaped over centuries. They are among the greatest stories in the world.
This is the story that first appeared at Level 5. Now it is told in full.

image.note: Illustration: a fisherman on a beach, a vast column of smoke rising from a brass jar he has opened, coalescing into a terrifying genie

pages.text: A poor fisherman cast his net four times. Three times he pulled up nothing useful: mud, a jar, bones. The fourth time he pulled up a sealed brass bottle. He opened it. A genie the size of a cloud poured out. 'I have been imprisoned for centuries,' the genie said. 'In the first century of my imprisonment, I swore to make my rescuer the richest person alive. In the second century, I swore to grant three wishes. In the third century, I swore to make my rescuer a king. But in the fourth century, my fury overcame me, and I swore to kill whoever released me, slowly and painfully. Prepare to die.'

The fisherman thought quickly. 'I do not believe you were ever inside that bottle,' he said. 'It is too small. You are far too large.' 'I was inside it,' said the genie, furious. 'I can show you.' And the genie, determined to prove the point, poured himself back inside the bottle. The fisherman replaced the seal immediately. 'Now we will negotiate,' he said.

The genie, having had several centuries to reflect on his temper, agreed to reasonable terms. The fisherman released him. The genie showed him where to fish to make his fortune, and departed without further threats. The fisherman fished there for the rest of his life and became, if not the richest person alive, at least a comfortable and well-fed one.
Moral: Cunning is more powerful than force, and a cool head in a crisis is worth more than either.

chapters.title: Ali Baba and the Forty Thieves

pages.text: Ali Baba was a poor woodcutter. One day in the forest, he hid in a tree as a band of forty thieves approached, led by their captain. The captain stood before a rock face and called out: 'Open, Sesame!' The rock opened. The thieves went in, came out with treasure, and rode away. Ali Baba waited until they were gone, then said the words himself. The rock opened.

image.note: Illustration: Ali Baba peering from behind a tree as the rock door opens before the thieves

pages.text: Inside was more gold, silver, and jewels than Ali Baba had ever imagined. He took as much as his donkeys could carry, went home, and told his wife. His wife borrowed scales from their wealthy neighbour, Ali Baba's brother Cassim, to weigh the gold. Cassim's wife smeared wax on the scales to discover what was being weighed. She found a gold coin stuck to the wax. Cassim forced Ali Baba to tell him everything.

Cassim went to the cave, said the words, and entered. In his excitement at the treasure, he forgot the magic words needed to open the door from the inside. The thieves returned and killed him. Ali Baba retrieved his brother's body, and with the help of a clever servant girl named Morgiana, outwitted the forty thieves one by one until none remained. Morgiana was rewarded with her freedom and a place in the family.
Moral: Cleverness and loyalty are more valuable than gold.

chapters.title: Sinbad the Sailor: The First and Second Voyages

pages.text: Sinbad the Sailor was a merchant of Baghdad who had made and lost several fortunes. He was about to make another. He loaded a ship with trade goods and set sail. On his first voyage, he stopped at what appeared to be a pleasant island to eat and rest. The island moved. It was not an island. It was an enormous sleeping whale. The whale dived. Sinbad swam for his life and was rescued by a passing ship.

image.note: Illustration: merchants and sailors fleeing across the back of a whale as it begins to sink beneath the waves

pages.text: He reached home, recovered his fortune, and promptly set out again. On his second voyage, Sinbad fell asleep on another island, a real one, and was left behind when his ship sailed without him. He was found by a roc, an enormous bird of legend large enough to carry elephants. He tied himself to the roc's leg with his turban and was carried to a valley full of diamonds and serpents. He filled his pockets with diamonds, tied himself to a carcass thrown into the valley by gem-hunters above, and was carried out on the back of an eagle. He reached home again, rather more diamond-rich than before.
Moral: Fortune favours the bold, and a quick mind can find an exit from almost any trap.

Sinbad's later voyages were stranger still. On one, his ship was wrecked and he alone survived, washed onto an island where an old man sat helpless by a stream and begged to be carried across on Sinbad's shoulders. Sinbad, kind-hearted, agreed, but once the old man's legs were locked around his neck, he would not get down, and rode Sinbad like a beast for days. Only by tricking the old man with fermented fruit did Sinbad at last shake him loose and escape.

On another voyage Sinbad was trapped in a valley and, by the custom of that place, sealed alive in a tomb. He survived by his wits in the dark and finally found a passage to the sea and rescue. Each time Sinbad returned home vowing never to sail again, and each time the pull of the horizon proved too strong. His voyages are really one long argument between comfort and curiosity, and curiosity, in Sinbad, always wins.
There is something important about the Arabian Nights that is easy to miss when you are caught up in the stories themselves.

image.note: Illustration: Scheherazade at a window at dawn, the king asleep behind her, the night's story still in the air

pages.text: The whole collection is a story about the power of stories. Scheherazade does not survive because she is stronger than the king. She is not. She does not survive because she is wealthier or politically powerful. She is not. She survives because she is a storyteller. She understands that a story told well, a story that makes you wonder what happens next, gives the teller a kind of power that nothing else can. The king cannot execute her because he cannot bear not to know the ending. Stories keep the teller alive. This is not just a metaphor. For two thousand years, storytellers have known it to be literally true.

Why has this one collection travelled so far and lasted so long? Partly because its tales are endlessly nested, a story within a story within a story, so that the reader, like the king, always wants to know what happens next. Partly because its heroes are so varied: poor fishermen and rich merchants, clever servant girls and foolish kings. And partly because at its centre stands Scheherazade, who defeats cruelty not with a sword but with the oldest tool humans have: a story worth staying alive to hear.

The Arabian Nights gathered tales from Persia, India, Arabia, and Egypt, and carried them on to Europe, where writers borrowed from it for centuries. Aladdin and his lamp, Ali Baba and his thieves, Sinbad and his voyages are known to children who have never heard the name of the book. That is the final proof of Scheherazade's victory: the stories she told to survive one more night have now survived a thousand years.
